content: The arrangement of electrons in atoms, organized by filling orbitals in order of increasing energy. Students often find this challenging but can understand it through analogies and systematic rules.
A pedagogical metaphor comparing electron configuration to filling seats in a theater, where lower energy levels (front seats) fill first before higher energy levels.
Quantum mechanical shells that electrons occupy, following sequence 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, etc. Lower energy levels are filled before higher ones.
Oxygen has configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁴, with 8 total electrons matching its atomic number. Used as a simple example to demonstrate electron filling.
The number of protons (and electrons in neutral atoms) in an element. For oxygen, this is 8.
Iron's electron configuration is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. A more complex example used to illustrate transition metal configurations and the use of noble gas shorthand.
Elements in the d-block of the periodic table that have partially filled d orbitals. Their electron configurations are more complex than main group elements.
A notation method that uses the previous noble gas symbol in brackets (e.g., [Ar]) to represent inner electron configuration, simplifying notation for large atoms.
The [Ar] notation represents the electron configuration of argon (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶), used as a shortcut in writing configurations for elements beyond argon.
When iron forms Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺ ions, electrons are removed from the 4s orbital first, despite 4s filling before 3d. This demonstrates the counterintuitive nature of ionization.
The counterintuitive principle that 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons during ionization, even though 4s fills before 3d during atomic build-up.
Electrons fill orbitals by energy level, not by principal quantum number. This explains why 4s fills before 3d but empties first during ionization.
The fundamental principle stating that electrons fill orbitals starting with the lowest available energy levels first (aufbau means 'building up' in German).
Rule stating that electrons spread out among orbitals of the same energy (degenerate orbitals) before pairing up, minimizing electron-electron repulsion.
Principle stating that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers. This limits each orbital to two electrons with opposite spins.
Set of four numbers (n, l, m_l, m_s) that uniquely describe each electron in an atom. The Pauli Exclusion Principle requires these to be unique for each electron.
Student analogy summarizing electron configurations as a complex seating arrangement for electrons, acknowledging the systematic but intricate nature of the rules.
The underlying quantum mechanical principles that govern electron behavior and configuration rules, providing theoretical foundation beyond simple analogies.
